utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. This is Thursday, September 10th, 2009, and I greet Mr. Praljak, as well as Mr. Prlic, Mr. Stojic, Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. Pusic. Of course I also greet Mr. Coric, and I hope that he will be back with us as soon as possible. I'm also greeting the Defence counsels: Mr. Stringer, his colleague -- his colleagues, and everyone helping us. Judge Prandler will be with us in a minute -- after the first break, actually. He has some business to attend to right now. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, let me issue an oral decision and then I will give my own opinion. Oral decision on the motion of the Prosecution regarding the cross-examination of expert witness Josip Jurcevic and Vlado Sakic. Let me read it slowly because it's quite long. On September 9th, 2009, the Prosecution filed a motion in which it is asking the Trial Chamber to grant it seven hours and 30 minutes for the cross-examination of expert witness Josip Jurcevic, who is planned to be heard from -- on September 14th to September 17th, and six hours and 30 minutes for cross-examination of expert witness Vlado Sakic, who is planned to be heard from October 5 to October 7, 2009. On September 10th, 2009, this morning, the Praljak Defence filed a reply to the Prosecution's motion, stating that it did not wish to have a position regarding the said motion. The Trial Chamber recalls that it has given a ruling as far as the time allotted to the cross-examination of these two expert witnesses in its two orders on the modalities governing the way the expert witnesses Sakic and Jurcevic would be heard, orders of April 22nd, 2009, and May 6th, 2009. The Trial Chamber also recalls that on April 14th, 2009, Prosecution had filed under Rule 94 bis a notice in order to be able to cross-examine the expert witnesses Sakic and Jurcevic without giving an indication on the time required for the cross-examination. The Trial Chamber first believes that the motion is in fact a motion to review the orders of April 22nd and May 6th, 2009, and decides to deal with it as such. The Trial Chamber considers that given that the motion is coming at a very late moment, it is in the interest of justice to issue -- to rule on this as quickly as possible, and therefore, believes that it is not important to listen to other parties. The Trial Chamber also notes that the Prosecution was not able to prove that there was an error made that would justify that the orders of April 22nd and May 6th would be revisited. Furthermore, Prosecution should have raised the grounds that it raises now in its notice of April 14th, 2009, and not now at this very late stage in the procedure. Consequently, the Prosecution did not prove the existence of any new element that might justify a review of these two orders. Therefore, the Trial Chamber decides that there's no need to reconsider these two orders and decides to dismiss the Prosecution's motion. The Trial Chamber recalls that the Prosecution will have three hours for the cross-examination of Josip Jurcevic and two hours for the cross-examination of Vlado Sakic. Personally -- on a personal note, I wanted also to add my own opinion, my personal opinion, which goes along with -- which is in line with what has been said. I note that the two expert reports were filed on April 3rd for Sakic - April 3rd, 2009 - and on March 13, 2009, for Jurcevic. I believe that when these reports were received on the very same day or in the days following it, the Prosecution should have read this report, studied it, and therefore, be immediately able to tell the Trial Chamber how long it decided it would need for the cross-examination. I note that the Prosecution filed its notice on April 14th without giving indication of the time required for cross-examination purposes. As a consequence, I believe, together with my fellow Judges in this Trial Chamber, that this motion came in too late and that there was no need, actually, to revisit our decision. So the Prosecution will have three hours for the cross-examination of Witness Jurcevic and two hours for the cross-examination of Vlado Sakic. I believe that our registrar has an IC number for the maps.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, thank you. 3D has submitted a list containing the exhibits and document numbers of the map used by witness Slobodan Praljak during the proceedings of the 8th of September, 2009. This list shall be given Exhibit Number IC1035. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me give the floor to Mr. Stringer. I believe that he has questions to put regarding these maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. Before I begin addressing just a few questions to the general, I don't think this will take too terribly long, Mr. President, in light of the remarks that have just been made by the Court's ruling in respect of the cross-examination and time for these two witnesses, I did want to inform the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution is reviewing the expert report that was more recently filed by the Petkovic team, and although we filed our notice last week saying that we wanted to cross-examine him, it's a very lengthy report, appears to be supported or -- or linked to a huge volume of documents as well, and so I want to inform the Trial Chamber that we're in the process of analysing all that and that we are going to provide the Trial Chamber with what we think is our estimate of the time that we would need for cross. Having just gotten the report we're not in a position to do that now, but we're going to try to do that as expeditiously as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for this effort. The faster you can tell us the time required for cross-examination the -- that way the Defence can give us its position on this and the Trial Chamber can issue a decision on it quickly and that way everything will run smoothly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Now, Mr. President, if I could just make one statement on behalf of the Prosecution in respect of all of the maps, because I think that -- I don't know how productive it would be and -- in fact, I doubt that it would be very productive at all at this point given the many, many hours that the general has been testifying on direct and on cross-examination for the Prosecution now to sort of re-enter a cross-examination on the subject of which party attacked who on any given day. Several of the maps - and the Trial Chamber has those - several of the maps make assertions about HVO attacks in Mostar on the 9th of May, for example, or in Busovaca, or in any other number of places, and rather -- I think, you know, we could spend days and weeks on a cross-examination of just that issue, and I think that in light of all that's been said and the length of time that the general has been testifying, if I can just note for the record that the Prosecution does not accept the characterisation that the general has placed on the maps as to which party initiated or attacked on any given day. It's certainly the general's evidence, and we expect that the Trial Chamber will consider that together with all of the other evidence in the case and reach its own conclusions to the extent it feels it needs to do so about which party launched an attack on any of the locations that are noted in the maps. I'd simply add that the adjudicated facts that the Trial Chamber accepted prior to the trial do include statements or findings about a couple of the combats or military attacks that -- that are referred to in the indictment, and rather getting -- rather than getting into the details of all that, we'd invite the Trial Chamber to reconsider the adjudicated facts, consider all the evidence in the trial, and to accept the Prosecution's statement that it disputes the general's assertions about who started or who launched an attack on a given day, because I'm not going to take all the time to go into that at this point. I do have a few limited points --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is totally improper at this point. I believe we're hearing closing argument. If there had been an objection with respect to the maps it should have been made two days ago. It's highly untimely at this point to sort of hear the testimony and then make a general comment. As far as adjudicated facts are concerned, you know, there is a presumption that they're correct, but, you know, it's a rebuttable presumption, and so -- but again I don't think these are very helpful comments at this time of the proceedings. They should have come much earlier. And might I remind the Prosecution that it was at the Trial Chamber's insistence that the maps be dealt with at this stage. Clearly this is not the time to be arguing this. Now, if the Prosecution has questions regarding the maps, I would suggest that they go forward with their questions. Otherwise, you know, I have a standing objection to this sort of lecturing at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, what you said is not noted on the transcript. You already said that, and Mr. Karnavas, I believe, gave us the position of the Defence, so now you can go ahead and put your questions to Mr. Praljak if you have any questions regarding they maps. We heard the Defence, and the Judges will rule in the end. Mrs. Pinter was standing up. I hadn't seen -- does she want to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, and everybody else in the courtroom. I just wanted to say I agree with what Mr. Karnavas said, and I would like to add that the indictment has not been changed in any way. It was in its original as the accused received them in April. According to the contents of the indictment, it's very important who attacked what and when, because it is on that that -- whether it's the HRH -- or, rather, it concerns the HR HB and whether a joint criminal enterprise exists or not, whether it was a plan to launch attacks or whether it was a response to attacks. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The position of Mrs. Pinter is now also noted on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to state at the address of Mr. Karnavas that what I understood the Prosecutor as saying, with too many words, I would concede that, was, "If I don't challenge now, that doesn't mean I change my position." And I think so far it is acceptable. It's not really -- I did not listen, as it were, to any argument beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But that goes without saying. They don't have to address everything we always say. I mean, I think that's a given, but I understand they need some time to be overly cautious, and I assume that that was the intention. I'm just -- from a technical point of view I had to raise my objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I quite accept that. And, Mr. Karnavas, if you allow me an observation, if we could strike off all the words that have been said in this courtroom since 6 -- since April 2006, I think we'd be through far with the administration of evidence. I think it's a normal thing that we say a bit more, that would be absolutely necessary, be it in the courtroom, be it outside. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer. I also welcome Mr. Karnavas. He's now with Mr. Prlic's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I did use too many words. We're probably being overcautious, but we finished our cross-examination in a manner of speaking earlier. It's not clear to me what the status of this is. I suppose it's a re-cross, but I did want to make that remark for the record, and I apologise if I took too much time doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, we're only going to look at a few of the maps and the first one is your map number 3. Do you have that one in front of you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And just a quick question on this, because this, for the record, is labelled as "Joint Activities of HVO and ABiH for the Period June to October 29th, 1992"; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, I do apologise, but may we have the map either on the ELMO or on e-court, because otherwise the other accused can't follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sure. Let's put it on -- the ELMO, I think is the best. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, General, first question is, and we'll talk about this more in a minute, the date of October 29th, 1992. Is that the date -- is that date significant here because that's the date when Jajce fell?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And again just to -- I want to be sure I understand correctly what this is. Here what you've noted in this map or what you say are all the locations where the ABiH was fighting together with the HVO against the VRS, or these are all places where the ABiH and the HVO were -- were holding the -- the front line against the VRS; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not quite. This is important, because the -- well, the attacks on Jajce were already going on as well as the attacks on Posavina to secure the corridor that the Serbs needed. So in these two enclaves, Gorazde being one of them, here, and the Srebrenica enclave with Bratunac, there was no HVO there. However, in Sarajevo and all the other area, as well as Bihac and this area here was covered by the HVO, and in places the HVO together with the BH Army, and in other places the BH Army was on its own.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the colours denote that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it seems evident but I'll just ask it: The map does not show locations of conflict between the HVO and the ABiH. For example, Prozor, which had just been taking place during October.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you don't see that on this map. The conflict in Rama was an isolated conflict which was quelled very quickly, and it's not included on this map, but it is on another map.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And then now the next map is number 4. If you could put that one on the ELMO. And, General, if I understand correctly, this map is a snapshot of the 29th of October, 1992, or is this supposed to be November? That was my -- that was my first question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all right. It says what it is, "Joint activities after the fall of Jajce," and simultaneously -- well, the map should be far more complicated. If you wanted them to show how the territory was lost in Posavina, in an offensive launched by the VRS which went on for months. So this on this particular day or after that day, the VRS took control of Jajce, liberated or expanded its corridor and all that remained -- no, I'm here. Jajce fell, and the VRS managed to make a large corridor here in Posavina, but the HVO enclave remained in the area as drawn into the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I have a technical question. I should have put it to you yesterday, but I didn't think about it. The front line is red for the Serbs, and for the ABiH and for the HVO it's in green and blue, but is it continuous? Is it a continuous front line, or is it discontinuous, because here you drew a continuous line, which means that there was no passage possible through the front line. It was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The front line is continuous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, General, this being the 29th of October, after Jajce fell, then what we see in the area just to the east, south-east of Jajce you've got a blue line there for an HVO position, or HVO part of the line, and then you've got green above it and green below it. So is that how it was after the 29th of October, you had the HVO holding one part and the ABiH holding other parts?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next map is number 5. I just want to come back again to -- this is a point, General, that I asked you about earlier or during the cross-examination. This map, you say, relates to -- well, this one's different than the other two because this one actually depicts conflict between the HVO and the ABiH; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. In two areas. What happened was that there was active defence on the part of the HVO in the Uskoplje area, and that went on from the 11th to the 23rd of January, and the other thing was the attack by the BH Army where the links between the HVO and Travnik and Vitez were cut off, and on the other side Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Let's focus on number 1 first, which I believe relates to Gornji Vakuf or Uskoplje; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, you've got, and we can see it, the arrows point to a circle or an oval that's coloured orange, and the orange appears to relate to the VRS, and so it's not clear to me what you're telling us is based here or is located here in Gornji Vakuf or just east of Gornji Vakuf. This orange oval on the map, are you saying that that is some sort of a VRS presence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stringer. The VRS is red and the orange colour was chosen for the simple reason that in the detention centre we don't have many colours at our disposal in terms of pins, and so this colour, the colour orange, is readily visible. It just shows that there was a conflict there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything else is an elaboration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And again, General, this map does not show any HVO guns or artillery position at Makljen Ridge during the period of January 11th to the 23rd; correct? You've not indicated that on the map.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not indicated on that map, and apart from that I never said that at Makljen there was any artillery -- there were any artillery pieces belonging to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I know you never said that or -- General. It's something that you were asked about on cross-examination, however. Maybe we should go back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask if we could put it up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would object, I think, on this line of questioning. It is clear that on this map the author of the map, General Praljak cannot mark whatever anybody imagined. The question regarding map earlier, I mean the assignment, and the description of the map is quite clear. So possibly the Prosecution may produce another map and show the guns or hospitals or power plants or forestry company, whatever they want. The request to Mr. Praljak was, as far as I remember, show us, and this was one of the requests, show us division as it was shown here. This is Mr. Praljak's knowledge and understanding. This is the method he choose. So if the Prosecution want to have anything else on this map, let's prepare another map. Let's bring the witness and present it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, this you did daunting task when marking all these maps, but I must say, and I did notice yesterday but I said nothing because I was waiting for Mr. Stringer's question. You didn't really meet my. Demands, you know. I did want to see on the one hand the front lines, but when you look on the transcript what I was going you to do, I also wanted you to position the ABiH and the HVO units. I did specifically say that, and I also asked you to write down the name or the numbers of all these units so that we could really see how things were at the time, and you did not do this. Maybe you forgot to do it, but if you had done such a detailed work on Gornji Vakuf, we would have seen exactly where the HVO was positioned and where the ABiH was positioned. I had a number of reasons for putting this request to you, because in the indictment there are military attacks that are mentioned, but not just that. We also had the incident at Makljen Ridge, and I wanted to know where the units were positioned, and on these maps we cannot see where the units are positioned. The Prosecution is telling you that you -- why did you draw these three arrows towards Gornji Vakuf. What does it mean exactly, because it doesn't shed much light on anything. We see that an attack is going on, you're telling us that it's the ABiH. Fine. Where were they, at the top of the arrow, at the other side of the arrow? Which ABiH units were you talking about? We don't know. You maybe don't know either. It doesn't shed much light. So let's say that you -- you met my demands but only halfway, unfortunately. I did -- hold it against you, of course, it was a daunting task that I asked you to do, but it's only -- you only did 50 per cent of it, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to answer Mr. Kovacic. I think his objection is justified for two reasons: First, this is a map the scale of which does not allow to put artillery positions. I mean, you need one to 100.000 or less to really and truly do that. So it's not the realistic objection to the map. And second, Mr. Praljak has said there was no artillery on Makljen. I see no justification for bringing this question again especially on the basis of a map where it couldn't have been meaningfully shown anyway. So I would like you to go to another question, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at an exhibit -- it's one that we looked on this very topic earlier in your cross, General. We're going to -- I'm going to have to ask them to put it up on e-court. It's an exhibit that's in evidence. You've all looked at it before, P01183. General, now, this is Colonel Siljeg writing to the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade on the 18th of January 1993, and he says: "Given that this morning we have launched an attack on Gornji Vakuf from the direction of Makljen, there is heavy fighting going on over there, and therefore, we cannot perform the evacuation." General, I recognise the scale of the map is what it is, but when you're indicating here that there is an ABiH attack or when you're asserting that that's what is depicted in this map, the fact is that the map is false, and it was an HVO attack from the direction of Makljen that occurred during the very period of time that you have written this map for. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stringer. First of all, I would kindly ask His Honour Judge Antonetti to understand that this is what I understood with regard to the maps that I was supposed to draft. The number of units would require tens of huge maps because they're talking about hundreds of units of the BiH Army or the HVO, and if you ask me to draft very correct maps based on documents and my knowledge with regard to the conflict in Gornji Vakuf, I can do it to the best of my recollection and knowledge. It wouldn't be difficult. I can go back to the drawing table. I can go back to the witness stand, and I can testify again for an hour or two. That wouldn't be a problem to me. Second of all, I have shown a very precise map of Gornji Vakuf to an English major depicting the units of the BH Army on the map, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We've had -- you've got your opportunity to give us an extensive description of each one of these maps the other day, and I think that we've heard enough. We all know what your position is on these maps, General. You don't need to repeat yourself. I've asked you a question. I've put something to you, you denied it, you know the Prosecution position, so I'm ready to move on to the next map, and that's map --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because please -- please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General. General, allow Mr. Stringer to ask his questions. You know that Gornji Vakuf is important. I was expecting from you a first map that would have shown the positions prior to the attack, be it HVO or VRS units, but the position the HVO and BH Army units in the region before anything started, and you would have said, "This is where the HVO was. This is where the BH Army was." Then in a second map you would have shown us or you would have told us, according to you, the attack by the BH Army to take control of the Makljen Ridge. Then you would have shown a third map that would explain that following the attack by the BH Army the HVO initiated defensive action, and in fact this document could help to explain this, that is to say, following the Makljen Ridge attack then the HVO decided to conduct an operation against Gornji Vakuf, and you would have shown the third map, and on the third map you would have shown the position of the various units. Not a difficult exercise, especially inasmuch as the issue of Gornji Vakuf had been the subject of very heated debates, I remind you, and I thought that the maps would be very telling about this. Unfortunately, that is not the case except for what we see here with these three arrows saying the BH Army is attacking Gornji Vakuf. It's too late now, so let us listen to the Prosecutor ask his question, and answer his question to the best of your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. I apologise, General. General Praljak's Defence is not finished with its case, so we're going to call Zrinko Tokic from Gornji Vakuf, together with General Petkovic Defence. His testimony will be supported by the maps and all the other documents. This may be one of the reasons why the general did not provide any more detailed maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. This will be an opportunity to return to this question. Mr. Stringer, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to answer, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You did, General. You said, No. I put it to you that the HVO attacked -- we're getting French on the English channel, at least I am. General, I put it to you that based on this document, in fact, the HVO launched an attack as is reflected in this. You disagreed with me, and we talked about this previously on cross, and so I think we can move from it. We don't need to debate this any more. So the next map, the last map, is number 11. All right. General, this one you have as the situation on areas under control of HV -- of ABiH and HVO, July 30, 1993. Now, General, I want to focus on the blue part that runs roughly from Gornji Vakuf down to Stolac, that HVO territory, and the question is this, General: During the period of time that you were commander of the HVO Main Staff, weren't you responsible to protect civilians against crimes committed by HVO soldiers in that blue zone?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would object to the question. The Prosecutor has 15 minutes to ask questions about the maps. He now re-opens another issue, and it seems that he is cross-examining again. He was given 15 minutes to ask the general about positions depicted on the maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was quite surprised and startled when I heard you asking this question, because this is a question you've already put to him. You have put this question to him, and he responded, if memory serves. I don't have the transcript, but I still have a fairly good memory, in spite of my age. And he answered, "We are responsible -- we are responsible along the border, along the front line. The rest is not of our responsibility -- or under our responsibility, that's what he said, and the answer was quite clear." Now, starting from the maps, you're asking the question again. I think it's overdoing it. If he wants to answer, he can answer. His counsel is objecting, and I think that she is right to do so. The Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I would like to respond to that, Mr. President, with all due respect to the Trial Chamber. This is a question that was raised by Judge Trechsel in Tuesday's proceedings when we were all looking at this map, because the Prosecution submits that what's shown on this map is inconsistent with and contradicts the witness's testimony on this very point earlier when he claimed that the territory or the zone of responsibility was only the front line. Now, we've got a map that the general's produced that shows -- tells us that the ABiH, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the HVO had these territories under their control; and I think it's a fair question, and with respect, I think the general successfully avoided answering the question when it was put to him by Judge Trechsel. The general claims that he's only responsible for civilians on the front lines, the place where the blue meets the green. I think the Prosecution, under the circumstances, should be able to put to him that, in fact, he's responsible for protecting civilians throughout the blue area from crimes committed by HVO soldiers, something that he denied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, your question can be admissible. The problem is the definition that you're giving to the HVO. In your mind, do you mean the military HVO, or do you mean the HVO in the broader sense, meaning to say both the civilian and military understanding of the HVO? That is where the problem lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is a direct follow-up to the questions from Judge Trechsel, because as Judge Trechsel pointed out, the reference here is to the ABiH. That's the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And clearly what that tells us, or what we can conclude, in the Prosecution's view, is that the reference to the HVO is, of course, the military or the army component of the HVO, which is the equivalent of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, please answer the question since the Prosecutor is saying that since you said HVO as -- in terms of its military component, you should answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer's interpretation is not correct. The use of the word "control" is not literal here. It is an arbitrary expression, a popular expression, and in the interpretation provided by Mr. Stringer it doesn't make sense. The HVO did not conquer the territory. It was defending it. It did not occupy the territory. Therefore, it could not be responsible for the situation before the civilian authorities were established. So it was not responsible as it would have been in the territory conquered by it. The soldiers were, therefore, responsible for only what was happening on the front lines and around it depending on the configuration of the terrain, a hundred, 150 metres around it in order to protect its flanks. The rest does not have anything to do with the military component of the HVO, but the same applies to the BiH Army. What was happening in Tuzla or Zenica was up to the authorities there or the civilian police, and the same was true of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to point to the lack of precision in the translation of one part of General Praljak's answer in part -- in lines 7 and 8. The sentence in the two lines is not what the general actually said. The general said that the HVO Army could not be responsible for the situation as it would have been if the territory was occupied before the civilian authorities were established, and as I read the transcript, I'm reading in English, General Praljak, you can follow what was recorded and you can correct me. It says and I quote: [In English] "It could not be responsible for the situation before the civilian authorities were established." [Interpretation] It is not clear that the general was referring to a situation that would have been in place if the territory had been occupied; is that correct, General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The borders of the blue enclave is what was held by the troops, and the troops were responsible for that line and not for the territory in-depth, not in any case. I've already explained that, and I have nothing else to add to that. And the same applies to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, although I put the words under the control, the word control is -- defies translation. It is a word used colloquially when we say that somebody controlled something.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: A war was being waged between the two sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Last question on this: Both Gornji Vakuf and Prozor appear in your map to be very close to the area of the front line. So are you telling us that you, as commander of the HVO Main Staff, had no responsibility in respect of civilians who were located in Prozor or Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is exactly what I'm saying, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So on this map as you've indicated, then, Gornji Vakuf or Prozor, they're not quite close enough to the front line for you to be responsible for them. Is that your evidence, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, in Gornji Vakuf at the time the line went through the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. So let's talk about the -- the civilians on the HVO side of the line in Gornji Vakuf. You're telling us, General, that those civilians were not quite close enough to the line to fall under your responsibility if they were victims of HVO crimes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know what crimes you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, let's just assume that you've got Muslim civilians who are in a detention facility in Gornji Vakuf in the blue zone. Is it your testimony that they're still not close enough to the line to be your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have an objection to the lack of precision in the question. The question that refers to the front line, for example, in Gornji Vakuf, has to be more specific with regard to the time-frame.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, because the front line in January --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could be the area of conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to object to this kind of testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just referring to the line that the general just told us ran right through Gornji Vakuf. That's the line I'm asking him about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to draw your attention to the fact that the maps were drawn at your request to depict the front lines facing the Army of Republika Srpska, and that's why I'm asking when reference is made to front lines to be more specific, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the witness may be confused by the lack of precision in your question with regard to what kind of front line you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, you just told us that there was a line running right through middle -- right through Gornji Vakuf. That's the line I'm asking you about, that specific line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is obstruction, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Tag-team obstruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Before he said that this is obstruction, you should permit me to give a word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you have the floor. Your client wants to testify to tell the truth. Up until now he has led himself to the game of questions and answers. He has drawn up a map. He has positioned, according to him, the front line, the position of the BH Army, the position of the HVO, and he has indicated the zone of control. One can argue whether it's military control, whether it's civilian and military control. We're not entering into that discussion. The Prosecutor is then using the map to ask the following question about Gornji Vakuf. He's saying -- he's asking: Is Gornji Vakuf close to the front line? General Praljak answers, Yes. Then Mr. Stringer, who is a professional, goes on to ask the question whether there was a front line within or going through Gornji Vakuf. Mr. Praljak's answer was, Yes. Mr. Stringer pushed ahead with his questions because as a professional that's his job. Then Mrs. Alaburic got up and said, What front line are we talking about, the one with the Serbs or with the Muslims? Then Mr. Stringer again tried to make it clear what we were talking about. And now, Mr. Kovacic, you're interrupting to add something. And this is why I'm surprised. What is it you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept your words entirely and I'm not going to deal with the matter that Mrs. Alaburic dealt with. My objection is as follows: The question suggestion something impossible. What the question suggests is that on this map and the map of this scale, I don't have the whole map on the screen, I believe that the scale is 1:1.000.000 it would be impossible, technically impossible, to show on this map the separation line on Prozor. This is - I apologise - in Vakuf, and the question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. You should apologise. Your client has said this was where the front line was. Forget about the map. And on the basis of this, the Prosecutor asks a question. And it is obstructive to intervene and lead away from that, speak about the map. I'm sorry. Please, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Your Honour, the Prosecutor started with the map. It was not my client. The Prosecutor says this map and then Mr. Praljak answered. Let the Prosecutor asks whatever he wants. I don't have any objection. I'm just warning everybody that yesterday it was very clearly defined that the Prosecution would be allowed to re-cross about the maps, and I leave it in your hands, but when you have a map the scale of which is 1:1.000.000, you can't talk about details. Why didn't he draw cannons on a map? Yes, if the map is different why aren't there separation lines in Prozor. In Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, or Mostar, it makes no difference it's neither here nor there. Give us a different map, a different scale, and it will all be shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, the Trial Chamber believes that beyond the question we should have had a map with the front line, but Mr. Stringer's question is more theoretical. His assumption is that in Gornji Vakuf there's a front line. I think this is conceivable for everybody here present. And then he asked a question about the scope of responsibility of a military commander. It is a simple question, and, in fact, this question came to my mind as I was listening to the direction the questions were taking. So I allow Mr. Stringer to ask his question. Mr. Praljak can answer. He can either agree with what he says or he can object and say why, and then this will be on the record. Go ahead, Mr. Stringer, and ask your question, but be very specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the map here, your map number 11, is the situation on 30th of July, 1993. Now, I'm looking at transcript, page 21 -- actually, page -- top line of page 22, and you said: "Sir, in Gornji Vakuf at the time, the line went through the town itself." So my question, General, is: For Muslim civilians on the HVO side of that line in Gornji Vakuf, weren't they -- weren't you responsible to protect them against crimes from the HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. First of all, Mr. Stringer, after the fall of Bugojno --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, excuse me, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please I apologise. I apologise. There were no Muslim civilians except in very small parts on the side of the HVO. After such conflicts, what happens is the separation of peoples in the area. That's number one. Second of all, I was responsible for the civilians on the side of the BiH Army -- I was not supposed to bring two 203 mm cannons and level to the ground regardless of the civilian victims, the army that attacked them. I'm talking about the BiH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I'm talking and that's what I was responsible for.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think the general is having a conversation with his counsel now in a language that we're not getting in English, so --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I want to answer, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to keep you to -- what I'm interested in getting and the answers I'm interested in, because you're saying that you're not responsible for civilians who are some distance from the front line. So my question is: In Gornji Vakuf, how far from the front line that ran through the town -- what was the dividing point where you're no longer responsible for civilians in the blue zone?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is pointless, militarily pointless. First of all, there were no Muslims on that side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not share this statement, Mr. Praljak. The Prosecutor is saying Gornji Vakuf, but it could have been any other place or town, X, Y, or Z. Assume that it's a town or a city. There are two belligerent parties, A and B. In the zone where belligerent B is there is a civilian population that -- or, actually, on the side of belligerent party A. To make this even more clear, it's the BH Army and HVO. In a given town, a lady, elderly lady, who is Muslim has not left because she's deaf. She's still there. And the HVO comes along and seizes that territory and is fighting again the BH Army, and this unfortunate civilian woman is caught in the middle, and the theoretical question that the Prosecution is asking is to know whether in this hypothetical case the HVO, and the question could have been asked about the BH Army, it's exactly the same thing. So the question is: Do you have responsibility for protecting that civilian person? That is the question. The question is: Should a military commander protect a civilian who is in the combat zone in the area where his own units are positioned? That's the question. There's no trap intended.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not on your part, but I'm afraid that Mr. Stringer is trying to set a trap for me, and I'm trying to avoid it by answering accurately. It is true that if in a village the lines -- the front lines move, somebody's attacking, the other party is defending and there's a certain number of civilians there and the village is under fire either from one side by one army or parties that are inside the village, it is true that the commander is then responsible for civilians. And I showed you a document where I was involved in combat, and there was a village, and I relocated a certain number of villagers, together with their livestock, lest they should be killed in such a clash, that's true. But if in Mostar you have a line that follows down the Bulevar, the next building which is inhabited by Croats or Muslims, it's immaterial. They are there at their own responsibility, and they are under the civilian structures, civilian police, and so on. It is my task to lead the troops and to have them man the bunkers which are there. As for the civilians, nobody, myself included, can prevent them or force them from leaving the front line, but those Muslims and Croats remained, and they lived there on the right bank and on the left bank too. Now, it is the responsibility of the commander that proportionality of the combat… Well, how would I apply the principle of proportionality? My lads are being killed because we're under attack. Will I take out –- two 203 mm cannons, and destroy all their military targets including the bridge regardless of civilian casualties and so on. Or will I say: I will not fire on mortars that are positioned by the hospital, I will act restrictively. And it's a very difficult decision for a commander to act restrictively when your men are being killed and when they are asking you why we do not fire back more fiercely. I'm just trying to be very accurate in my answer here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You answered. You answered fully. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, also on the map, General, if we just move down along that front line from Gornji Vakuf down toward the south and east, then it's hard to find it here, but the fact is Prozor is also very close to this confrontation line, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not close. Prozor was 20 kilometres away from the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could you indicate the location of Prozor for us on map 11, the one that's on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't, not on this map. I can do it on another map. I can't do it here because I would only be guessing where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, we saw a report from Luka Markesic from August of 1993 where he said that all the Muslims were put into collection centres by Ilija Franjic to make room for incoming Croat refugees from Bugojno. Do you remember that report?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I don't recall that report any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That was P04177. If we could take a brief look at that. I'm almost finished, Mr. President. P04177.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will be on the screen in a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is re-cross. It has nothing to do with the maps. I am not opposed to the Trial Chamber allotting additional five hours to the Prosecution, but then let's revisit everything, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm just -- I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, be fair play. The Prosecutor is asking something using a map, and he's asking you where Gornji Vakuf is on this map. You say, "I can't show you." Maybe you're right. It's true the map is not very accurate. The Prosecutor is trying to move forward regarding Gornji Vakuf, and he's using this document which is now on the screen, dated August 14, 1993. You were Chief of the Main Staff at that -- at that time, and I'm sure he's going to ask you a question regarding this document in connection with the map, so please listen. Hear him out, you know, and then answer. I have no idea. I don't know what he's going to ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Markesic writes: "After the fall of the towns of Konjic, Bugojno, and part of Gornji Vakuf, settlement and welfare provision for refugees, women, children, and the elderly from those places is occurring in Prozor municipality. "Initially, they were put up in Croatian houses, but when the number grew they began to be settled in Muslim houses and villages. "Thus the entire Muslim population from Rama municipality is accommodated in three collection centres, Pogradje, Duge, and Lapsunj." And then it goes on to talk about things that were happening with those Muslims in those collection centres. General, tell us, the Muslims in those three collection centres, were they close enough to the front line to benefit from your protection, the front line that you put on this map here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Stringer, I don't agree with your interpretation of the closeness of the front line. Well, in military terms, it's a completely different matter. But this is 20 kilometres away from any front line, if you want me to be specific in terms of the distance. Even if it were 200 metres away from the front line itself, again it has nothing to do with the military. I was talking about distance from the front line and the protection that the military can accord in the depth of the territory, but it doesn't mean that if it's close to the front line the military will be responsible for providing protection. The fact that the military is trying to protect its back, its rear, and it's responsible for protecting it, and if somebody's there and remained there for unknown reasons, civilians refusing to leave, there were many cases where you had an old man saying, Well, I don't want to leave my home even if I get killed here. They refused to leave their houses, well, in those cases --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So your evidence, General, is that for the Muslims in these three collection centres, the HVO military had no responsibility to protect them; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not talking about the military police. I was talking about the HVO, the army, the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The commander of the HVO Main Staff had no responsibility in respect of these Muslims. Is that your evidence, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Although my script for the re-direct is going to be changed, but I would like this document, P04177, to remain on the screen, and I'll pursue a different script.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, would I like you to look at it and tell me who is this document addressed to? Who is the recipient of this report, if you can see.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult. The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. That's as much as I can read. The rest, the Croatian Defence Council --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Please look at the stamp.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Security and Information Service, SIS.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, could the general please look at pages 2 and 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And you can see that the document was sent to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no such document reached or was addressed to the Main Staff. And I said that ten times.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, I know, General, but this question was again asked, and that's why I also asked it. Let me just get organised. We'll try to be efficient. And right at the beginning I have to warn you, both you and myself, and Judge Prandler is not here to keep an eye on us, we have to make sure that everything is in the record. We must not overlap. So I will ask you to make a pause after I finish my question. So could you please open document P00312. This document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I'm still interested in this document. Let me read it, and I don't have to take sides, you know, either -- for this. I just have a document here on the screen, and I'd like to know whether it does reflect the military situation of the -- at the time, as well as the consequences of this military situation. That's what I'm supposed to do. Using a document and using what -- what everyone is saying, I will have to draw conclusions. This is a report made by the SIS. Obviously it's from some kind of intelligence department, and the -- it's an assessment of the military situation by intelligence services, and it says on page 2 that MOS, obviously, is gathering its forces and that attack is probably under plan. If I had the map, of course, I could check where the ABiH position -- where the BH Army units are positioned in order to see whether they're ready to attack or not. Well, in this document I read that there's a great number of Croat refugees, that they left a number of municipalities in Bugojno and so forth and so on. I can read all that. Then also in this document, I read that the military police has decided to accommodate these refugees in flats where Muslims used to leave. So I'm wondering, you know, where these Muslims are. And when I read the document, I note that they've been sent to three collection centres. That's the situation as we can read it in the report. If this -- if the document is truthful and unbiassed, this is the situation that the military police, the army, and the civilians authorities had to deal with, as well as the Muslims who ended up in those camps. And you're tell us that you don't know of this document. Fine. We note that. But in a situation as described -- could you tell us whether the situation as described does correspond to what you think it was, what you felt it could have been given the situation that was unfolding at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I don't know the answer to that question because I was not aware of these events. So when on the 24th I came there, I was greeted by 20 or 30.000 refugees, and I passed through them, and I asked the troops to organise it, and I went down to the front line, to the theatre of war, and I claim that throughout that time -- well, there were some minor breaks, but there was an offensive going on at all times. I had some 20 units or so. I don't know how to explain this to you. The only way to do it is this: I went from one small unit to another small unit, and I fought side by side with them, reclaiming some small areas, losing other areas. I had no idea what was going on. How can I say something when I really have no clue. Then when I took a breather, I had to go down to Mostar to see what was going on. On the 14th and the 15th, there was an attack on the southern area of Mostar, and then it goes on and on for 200 kilometres. I was concerned about how to get weapons to Blaskic, whether the helicopters would be able to be air-borne, what would happen with the wounded, the funerals of those who were killed, whether the ammunition would arrive. I don't know how to answer. It is as if there were 50 hours in every day. I didn't know anything about that. I didn't know anything about that at the time. Of course, later on I read the same documents that you did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, your answer is on the transcript. Mrs. Pinter, I apologise for taking the floor, but since you wanted to put questions to the witness on this document and the Prosecutor had also dealt with it, I wanted to get to the very bottom of things.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise to my colleague Mr. Stringer, who was not given a list of documents. I wasn't aware of the fact that the list did not reach him. The computer did not work and we were doing it last minute, but now he has the list. All the documents are in e-court. Most of the documents are those that you used, and the binder is a big fat one because we're going to use it as some kind of aide-memoire. It doesn't mean that we're going to use each and every document so just to refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So, General, the first document that you have in front of you is P00312, and in the course of the cross-examination there were questions on the 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the counsel please slow down when reading numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So line 41421 to 422 about Franjo Tudjman 's positions on Herceg-Bosna and its relationship with Croatia, and then on the 16th of July, 2009, the 13th of July, 2009, and the 16th of July, and the topic was Franjo Tudjman, Gojko Susak, and I could say HR HB, HZ HB, and the Republic of Croatia. This document, P312, is -- responds to a document used by Mr. Stringer in his cross-examination, and that's the minutes taken in the office of the President, taken at a meeting in December 1991. The document is P0089, in December. This document, P312, is dated July 1992. General, let me ask you: Can you, on the basis of this document that you are acquainted with because you have seen it, it has been admitted as evidence in this trial, can you conclude anything about the intentions, positions, and views of Franjo Tudjman towards Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Could you appoint us to the parts of this document that help you do so?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was aware because I had my post in the VONS, the National Defence Council and in the defence ministry about the positions of the Croatian leadership, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, Gojko Susak, and all of us vis-a-vis Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the position was as follows. At page 1, this is what Franjo Tudjman says: So negotiations, recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Well, that had already been done. Here he says that Mr. Izetbegovic is the one who wants a unitary state. He is opposed to the cantonal organisation. This is something that he purportedly stated for Der Spiegel and that there were only representatives of the Muslim people in the leadership of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But, again, at page 3 where Boban says: "It's always equal rights. We are not in favour of a war if a peaceful solution can be found no way." And at page 5, again, Franjo Tudjman says: However we have to say this -- at page 5, Franjo Tudjman says: Should the convention of the HDZ be held, the HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina? It is up to you to decide. So the leadership of the HZ HB, the representatives of the people, are independent. The Republic of Croatia helped the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or, rather, Bosnia and Herzegovina, not counting the areas inhabited by Serbs, but Muslims and Croats with equal amounts in the same manner and in a way it treated it as a sovereign state with accepting an international position of Bosnia-Herzegovina indicating that the three peoples within Bosnia and Herzegovina should get organised and agree on a relationship that would guarantee equal rights. The Serbs didn't want to do that. Muslims didn't want -- didn't want to do that either, politically, ideologically, and later on also militarily, and it also follows at page 6.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, time is really precious for us. In this document, it is stated that Stipe Mesic was present. My question to you as regards Stipe Mesic is this: To the best of your personal knowledge, your contacts and subsequent knowledge that you obtained having read the transcripts and documents, in the course of 1991, 1992, and 1993, while Stipe Mesic was in HDZ holding high positions within the Republic of Croatia, did he ever oppose publicly the policy pursued by the Republic of Croatia or the Croatian HDZ towards Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never anywhere. So in meetings at the military and defence council -- and here he says at page 6 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness is kindly asked to slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he goes on to say what everybody knows. We recognise the sovereignty of Bosnia-Herzegovina and so on and so forth. At that time -- through this time, he never ever mentioned anything that would indicate that he was distancing himself or that he disagreed with some conclusions or way of thinking, and he never mentioned any agreements between Slobodan Milosevic and Franjo Tudjman in Karadjordjevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I suggest that we should move on. Our new document that I'm going to show you is 3D03748.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, Mr. Mesic has taken the floor on page 6. This is important given his character. You know, it's important to know exactly what he says. And all the words he says must absolutely be weighted and assessed. I note that he says that the authority was destroyed. He must be referring to the authority and the organs over in Sarajevo, which are no longer competent, or maybe he's referring to the authorities of former Yugoslavia. And then he says that the HVO has set up of some kind of authority. There are places where civilian organs were elected, where -- and there is authority. And he says: "We recognise the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we also recognise the organs of power who were elected, which were elected." Now, when we look this -- when we scrutinise all this, does this mean that he is recognising the HVO in all its components? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, he recognised some forms of HVO for a very simple reason, because the war had destroyed in some areas, completely destroyed any possibility for the functioning, and that is why things happened in Sarajevo. The Assembly wasn't functioning. The government was reformed. It became a single ethnic -- mono-ethnic government. The members of the government would change like waiters, and this is how it was, but it is undoubted that Mr. Mesic accepted and recognised the HVO government as an interim government for the duration of the war and until the internal structure of the state is agreed; but the borders of the country, the legitimacy of the borders and the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state was not disputed at any point. It was uncontrovertible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The general would like us to take a break, and it is our time to make a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's break as usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, Franjo Tudjman and his ideas and objectives with respect to Bosnia and Herzegovina, that's the subject that we discussed a number of times during the examination, and his intention to divide Bosnia and Herzegovina and his relation towards Alija Izetbegovic, but first of all, let's look at a brief video. It's a programme, a film by Croatian Radio Television by journalist Goran Milic. It's called "A Visit to Turkey," and it was broadcast in June or July this year. We obtain the tape through the Ministry of Justice, the Department for International Co-Operation and Legal Assistance and Co-Operation with International Criminal Courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just for the record, it's our understanding that this exhibit, as well as three other ones that are on this -- the list, is not on the Defence 65 ter exhibit list. So I just note that for the record in the event that it's tendered at a later time or -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's true that it's not on the 65 ter list. First of all, because it was broadcast in June this year. So it couldn't have been on the list. However, as I understand it, we are now in the redirect stage where the Defence can use documents that it has in its possession in order to challenge the allegations made by the Prosecutor during cross-examination. We were not able to know on the 31st of March, 2008, what the Prosecutor's cross-examination would be like and which documents we need to have on the list in order to challenge his allegations, and therefore, I think that the Defence has every right to show the video and to use documents that are not on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Pinter, for the procedure to be observed you should say that during the cross-examination the Prosecutor at such and such a page asked the question and that you, therefore, believe there's an additional question to be put in relation to the reply. Otherwise, it remains a bit vague. You're saying that Mr. Stringer spoke of Mr. Tudjman, but we don't know exactly what you're referring to, so you have to be very specific in your reference.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Obviously the problem was with me, because at the very beginning, with P00312, I referred to the date of the cross-examination. I quoted the pages of the cross-examination, and I said that it related to matters regarding Franjo Tudjman's views of the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. So this is a block, a set of documents or exhibits on Franjo Tudjman, Gojko Susak, the Republic of Croatia, and the HZ HB. It was my mistake that in order to save time I did not give the same date and pages as the reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the video now, please. I'd like to ask the registrar to place the transcript on the screen, and it is 3D03748.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we cannot view the video and the transcript -- [French on English channel]. Yes, Your Honour. The way the courtroom is -- is featured is that we cannot view both the video and the transcript at the same time. It's either one or the other. Currently the video is on the screen. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we'll play the video. Everybody has the transcript. It's on e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they do not have the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel. The Prosecution doesn't have the transcript either. We don't have a hard copy of any of these exhibits. I wasn't going to squawk about it too much, although I think it appears binders have been made for others. But in any event, we don't have the transcript or any of the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they cannot interpret without the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the examination-in-chief of General Praljak we offered to print out for the Prosecutor all the exhibits we intend to use. The Prosecutor said at the time that he does not use a hard copy but the electronic version exclusively, and guided by that we didn't print anything out. Of course it wouldn't have been a problem to make an extra copy of the hard copy version, but since during the examination-in-chief the Prosecutor said he only accepted it on e-court, then it was my mistake -- it is my mistake for not doing this. My colleague Mr. Kovacic has always -- has told me that it has always been the case, that we always work that way, but this brings me into a somewhat difficult position, but Mr. Stringer has the entire list of documents and can look at them on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, in the interview -- in the video it's Mr. Demirel's interview, and I think there will be an interpretation of what he says in Turkish, I understand. So let us see the video and we'll see what the situation is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It seems we have some technical problems now and that it is not possible to play the tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, while we're waiting for the video to start --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Pinter, we can't see it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: "Ten years ago we went to the funeral of Franjo Tudjman. He was the only European president to be there. Today you think also it was a wise decision? "Yes, I think it was a wise decision, because I know him very closely. He was a man of his people. He loved his people. And then he just worked for his people, and then I -- I appreciate and I admire his determination that the Croatia should become an independent country and Croatia should be standing on her own feet, and the Croatia should -- one day should become a part of Europe. And then I have seen the goodwill of Croatian people, and the Croatian administrators. They -- first of all, late President Tudjman was very clever and a very wise man, and then things developed, and after President Tudjman, the President Mesic is doing very well, and now the -- there is peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina. "This show that we are doing is not so political. I like what you said about President Tudjman, but it's more personal. I see you ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, do you have personal knowledge that the former President, President Demirel, paid visits before the events, before President Tudjman's funeral?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not once -- well, President Tudjman, as far as I remember, also travelled to Turkey, and President Demirel and President Tudjman together, I think it was at the end of 1993, in May, formed a joint delegation of the Croatian and Muslim people with the assignment of going to Herceg-Bosna and the Mostar area to make another attempt to try and prevail upon the politicians down there to calm the situation down and to reach a compromise which would put a stop to the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to the next document now, which is P01158, and it is the presidential transcripts of the 15th of January, 1993. It's already an exhibit, and we talked about those minutes so many times that I didn't make any special references to the pages, but it is a document, which relates to the meeting held in President Tudjman's offices where Mr. Izetbegovic was present, as well as Lord Owen and many others that we have mentioned during these proceedings. I'd now like to ask you, General Praljak, to go to page -- well, to save precious time, the page number in Croatian is ERN number 01322250. And in English it is page 8 of pages 55. As we're still on the topic of President Tudjman -- have you found the page, General? 2250 are the last digits. You've spoken at length about the document already with relation to the 15th of January and the issuance of an order and the circumstances under which the alleged order on resubordination was given, and I'd now like to ask you to focus especially on the portion which speaks of Franjo Tudjman and his views of Bosnia-Herzegovina and relations within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this conversation, as indeed a series of other documents that have been admitted into evidence, is once again testimony to the crystal clear political option on the part of the leadership of Croatia led by Dr. Franjo Tudjman on the subject of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the war there, and he reiterates here, since Mr. Izetbegovic does not agree with the corridor, the situation around the corridor, which according to the Vance-Owen Plan was given to the Serbs and says that if the Serbs are given that corridor and the Serbs don't want to negotiate without it, that he was in favour of war. And Dr. Tudjman says -- well, we're in this kind of situation. Are we going to continue waging a war or not? And he goes on to say that he doesn't see any possibility of we, meaning Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, would win the war without it -- extending it for years and suffering enormous losses. And he says this strengthens our conviction that a policy of peace should be pursued, because peace means, he says, a certain amount of compromise. And then he goes on to say that in Posavina there were 138.000 Croats, and now with the actions of the Army of Republika Srpska in that smaller enclave that we saw on the map there are only 13.000 people left. And now these people can't go back because of the Serb tanks and cannons and guns. And Mr. Izetbegovic goes on to speak over the following pages that I'm leafing through now because I'm well aware of what was said during the conversations, anyway, President Tudjman goes on to say that he agrees that the Serb should be forced to reach a compromise, but he also says that Mr. Izetbegovic quite simply is seeking for war. And Franjo Tudjman says, Wait a moment. We can't continue the war for two or three years. Croatia is not prepared to participate in that at all cost. He says that Croatia has suffered enough. And then he says something very important, and it is this: There's a problem. Two million Serbs are in the west, half a million of them are in Croatia, the rest are in Bosnia, and he says, We cannot close our eyes before this fact. He's not waging a war against the Serbs. We're not in favour of war. Therefore, Croatia has to turn toward the problem of dealing with its economy and so on and so forth, the problems that face it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, in that same transcript Gojko Susak was mentioned, so I'd like to ask you to turn to ERN page number 1322293. The last digits are 293. And in the English version it is page 51 out of pages 55.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gojko Susak also says that they discussed that famous document that the Prosecutor has termed "ultimatum," and that the document was discussed in Geneva, and he says, Well, you down there. You have to reach an agreement. Because he's talking about a different state and that they should be -- they should know who does what. And he says that he can't understand what is contentious in all of that and that everything was in the common defence interest. And then I'll just quote the last sentence. He goes on to say, "Well, you're killing yourselves down there." So he's thinking about the Muslims and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina from the aspects of a different state and then he says, You don't need the Serbs. You don't need the Serbs to fight you because you're going to kill each other.
