And I have to tell you, madam Pinter, that the meeting of the 13th with high-ranking French delegation where I present my views and I say in crystal terms over there that the war will continue and I go on to explain why it will continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Praljak kindly be asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the talks that we had, Mr. Izetbegovic did not give up on the war option. Unfortunately, when he couldn't gain a victory over the Serbs and Franjo Tudjman says that that's impossible because they're strong and the international community didn't want to see that either, then he says the BH Army turned towards the weaker side, that is to say, toward the HVO, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, in fact. So that is the basis of this whole story and the crux of the relations between the two parties. Never a desire for a state, never a desire for a war. Boban speaks about peace here. We weren't in favour of the war, we in Croatia as a system for defence, neither in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we spent a great deal of time and effort to prevent a war with the BH Army, but I think that certain structures, the powers that be, forced Mr. Izetbegovic, because when he talks about Brcko here, he says, Here we have it. What can I say about Brcko when they died over there? In Dayton it became a district ultimately. It could have become a district earlier on and then the problem would have been solved, but there was no desire for a compromise until we had this balance of forces with thousands of dead, and unfortunately peace arrived just when we could see who was able to defeat whom. That's the logic of war. Nobody managed to settle this with peace negotiations. But at least we saw who advocated what.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Staying with the topic of Franjo Tudjman and the relationship between Bosnia-Herzegovina and vice versa, the BH's relation, its politicians towards Croatia, we have P07500, the document in front of you, which is a document which on the 9th of August this year --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreters are asking you to slow down a little bit. Thank you, Mrs. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I will do my best, and I do proffer my apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So the document is P07500. It was used in the cross-examination by Mr. Stringer on the 9th of August, 2009, and that's recorded at 43470, lines 16 through 25. It's a report on the movement of refugees of the HR HB, the office for refugees and displaced persons. And from this document the Prosecutor used only a couple of tables that were shown to you, and now I would like you to go to page 15 of this document, which is ERN -- yes. The pages are paginated. It's the same page in the English translation, page 15, line 2. As you can see, General, at page 15 it is stated that -- in this report that Muslims violated the Christmas cease-fire, which was -- concluded with the Croats with the approval of the international community and the representatives Ejup Ganic and Silajdzic are openly telling the public that the cessation of war in central Bosnia would not happen in a very long time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: The counsel is kindly asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What was Ejup Ganic's function in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1993 and 1994? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a member of the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I think that he was in a way the number two person in politics together with Silajdzic well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did he visit the Republic of Croatia in 1993 and 1994 to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993 he even came to see me. I met with him. We talked about the arming of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and even at that time he presented the same views. In fact, he requested weapons, but his political views were as is indicated here, and that is that if they would not be able to defeat the Serbs they would turn on us, particularly in Central Bosnia, and then they would move westwards down the Neretva River valley. And they had those vague plans to reach Ploce, so not the corridor down to Neum but to Ploce, and Ploce is in the territory of the Republic of Croatia. This is something that Sefer Halilovic published in a book of his, so it was an insane idea. There was some information to the fact that they were making deals with the Serbs for the BH Army to take of course with the approval of course that they would take the area from Ploce to Neum and then the Serbs would take Dubrovnik. And finally it resulted in the September 1993 agreement the military agreement between the VRS and the BH Army, between their political elites, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would like you to look at document 3D03751. It's a press briefing for Monday, the 3rd of January, 1994. The page is 10 of 14 in the English version. It begins with, "Sarajevo, 2nd of January, 1994." You -- General, you have the Croatian translation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It's a report filed by the Reuters News Agency, and I would like to draw your attention to the second paragraph at page 10. And that would be page 12 in the English version. So you have the Croatian translation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So you can use it. It's right at the end. So can you tell us, what kind of report is this and whether those allegations are identical to the allegations contained in the documents that we had -- have looked at, and that's P07500.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it just testifies to the same thing that I knew on the basis of those conversations. Ejup Ganic was a hawk so to speak in the politics there, and he advocated the taking of the Lasva Valley, and his words are quoted here that we would ensure our existence there to a certain extent. In other words, they were conquering space for them, territory, and that's how the attacks started on the Lasva Valley, and then of course they extended to the Neretva River valley as times went by. But I claim that in late 1992 there was already, according to all the information that I had at my disposal, a very strong core within -- well, there were not all of them there, but within the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, for a certain territory that the Muslim people could not get territory by defeating the Serbs, but it could do so by defeating the Croats.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Ejup Ganic also said or, rather, he made it known that his forces are not ready to stop fighting and he said that Muslims intended to take control, to wrest control away from the rebel Croats over the rich valley of the Lasva River in 1994 either by armed force or negotiations. "If we take the Lasva Valley, we have closed the circle and ensured our survival, existence, up to a certain extent." If we look at three documents -- once we've looked at three documents in a row, I will ask you questions so that we have the whole picture. Could you please look at 3D03752. It's again a report published on the 26th of June, 1993, in the "Independent" newspaper. You have the Croatian text. I would like to draw your attention here to the end of this article where it says -- just a moment. I don't have a marked copy. "In Sarajevo, Ejup Ganic." It's the third paragraph in English, and it's the fourth -- it's the fourth paragraph in Croatian. "Ejup Ganic, a member of the president and a close ally of Mr. Izetbegovic issued a dire prediction that the war in Bosnia would last another 15 years and would be accompanied by terrorist attacks if the world helped to finish off Bosnia." And so the date is the 26th of June, 1993. And now I would like us to look at 3D02591. So this document, 3D02591 was used by His Honour Judge Antonetti when he asked questions on Tuesday, the 7th of September, and it's tied in with the expert report filed by Mr. Gorjanc. So I'm just giving a reference for the question. It's at line 39 -- it's at page 39, line 10 of our daily transcript. The date is the 21st of October, 1993, and it's about -- it's an intercept involving Zuka and Alija Izetbegovic. Now, General, who is Zuka?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zuka was a commander in the BH Army whose units took part in the offensive Neretva 93 in Konjic, Jablanica, and Mostar areas. And now I would not like to go into the question of who committed the massacre in Grabovica and the one in Doljani and Uzdol and so on. It's not the subject --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: No, not at this moment, but I would like you to look at page 1, last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, a little correction to the transcript, I think. On page 52, line 7, the date of this is indicated as 21st of October, 1993. I think that's what you actually said, but what I read in both versions would be 21st September.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the 21st of September. Thank you, Your Honour. Obviously I misspoke and said October. And the date is important, the 21st of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, this last sentence on page 1 of this document -- well, let me explain first. This -- this is what Zuka says: "We don't have what Alija Izetbegovic says." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: But from what Zuka says, can we -- are we able to know what the discussion's about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with a great deal of certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Zuka says: "Sefko says that you ordered us to hold all war operations towards the Croats." And then Zuka goes on to say: "Mr. President, I -- the last time I came to see you we talked. You're our commander and we respect you. That's without a doubt. Sefko tells me over there that you told him something that wasn't specific. I have no reason to believe him, because I don't see anything written down on paper, and that is why it's good that you called." And Zuka goes on to say: "Mr. President, we will soon meet, but I would like to tell you, I think it would be a happy piece of news for you, and as far as Stolac and those parts down there are concerned, Dubrava, et cetera, and the rest, rest assured that we have the force and strength, and not only that, we also have the strength for Neum, and if they are impertinent, behave improperly, we will take Grude and Listica from them. We will take everything from them, Mr. President. We're not far away from Listica, Mr. President. We can do it, and we see that we can do it." Now, Listica, what's that, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I have one more document, and after that I'll ask you a question on all these together. The next document is P05162, and I think it's in front of you. I think it's under seal. I'm not quite sure, so can we have it on Sanction, please. Thank you. The topic of Uzdol was referred to on pages 43852 of the 25th of August, 2009, and 44179 of the 1st of September, 2009. The pages are 44210 and 44179, yes. General, in item 2 of this report titled "Political Situation," it is noted that -- well, it relates to the situation in Prozor, which as it says, Peacefully accepted the Uzdol massacre, they took it in their stride and have not to date abused the town's Muslim community. Now, this is a document of the 17th of September, 1993, General. Looking at this document now, can you link it up with Zuka and what was said, that he wouldn't stop, and what Ganic said about leaving Central Bosnia? That's my first question, and I have another question after that. And that question is as follows -- perhaps I can ask it straight away. Do these documents show that the HVO, the armed forces of the HVO, were in a strong offensive?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Defensive.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I said offensive. Does it show that the HVO was in an offensive, and the general's answer was, No, it was in a defensive.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BH Army was in an offensive.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes this topic. You wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Nika, you asked me whether this document links -- no. The BH Army has the right, according to war law, to attack the HVO, and that's what it does. Whether it has the right or not, well, I don't know. It's an army. And from these documents it's clear that Ejup Ganic and many around him do not want peace. They want to reach Ploce, Ploce in Croatia. So that's the port. Not only the Neum corridor. Neum is unimportant in this -- in these situations. But the HVO, there's always somebody rebelling there. As far as that group of people is concerned, the Croatian Defence Council was a rebel structure. They -- in their eyes they were the sole legitimate representatives of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Muslims, and when they doesn't do anything to the Serbs, then they proclaimed us to be rebels because we were the minority ethnic group there, and following that logic you had to deal with the situation militarily. Now, as far as this document on Uzdol is concerned, I don't want to link up this and say who committed any crimes, but I was in Uzdol at the time. We had -- well, I was even involved in an action to defend part of Vakuf. We stopped that. We transported two tanks and prevented a further massacre in Uzdol with a counter-attack, and the fact that the -- well, the population didn't take anything in its stride. At that point in time I and many other people invested a great deal of effort to prevent the situation from escalating by talking and negotiating and that they shouldn't rise to this occasion. Quid pro quo doesn't exist, but if in a small village when there are no refugees, they have already left, there's just 200 people, and then when somebody kills 41 of those 200 people, a fifth, therefore -- or not a fifth -- yes, a fifth of the population, it's a terrible thing, and I claim that as a prevention the only thing we could do was to talk, to entreat, to have a heated discussion, and what we could do technically speaking was to protect the mosque, to place guards in front of the mosque, and to place guards in front of the religious leader, because symbolically if somebody wanted to retaliate those are the two things that they would choose for retribution, and then the situation calmed down. Now, how the situation was calmed down, if you weren't there you can't even dream of what the psycho-physical state of those people there was like with all the dead, when they're burying 41 people and tensions grew and you had to go back and do the same thing again to calm the situation down. But the Muslim offensive at that time had already been routed in a way, and so some people had more time to devote themselves to this problem. And quite frankly as a human being I am proud of my role in all that, because as we can say they took the massacre in Uzdol in their stride peaceably. Well, that's debatable how any people would take anything like that in their stride is a very debatable question. Now, as far as these documents are concerned Mr. Ganic says there will be a war and he is issuing threats. He says the French are supporting Bosnia but the government not. Now, which French, I suppose some people there, I don't know, he says the British are even worse.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Could you tell us the number of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down and speak one at a time for the benefit of one and all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says that the British are enemies to Muslims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Did you realise you were asked again for the fifth or what times to slow down when speaking. You go on like a motorcycle -- racing motorcycle. It simply doesn't work. I don't understand that you have not understood this after four months of testifying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you, Judge Trechsel, and it is true what you say, but unfortunately it's not something that you understand but something that you cannot understand. Your mind understands it, but the body doesn't, so I fully understand it. And after all this time I simply cannot control the rate of my speech, so I'm guilty as charged but not because I'm stupid and because I don't understand, but because I -- well, I would like that to be repeated. So in this document Mr. Granic said that the British government that they hate the Islam, so he's talking about Islam, not Bosnia-Herzegovina. He says that Abdic, of course the one who won the most votes for the post in the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina is flexible and would be amenable to a compromise but that Mr. Izetbegovic and I say that it was under the pressure of his radicals for the most part couldn't do it although I still say that without the radicals his political options would have been different. So that's all I have to say on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. I made a pause less we should overlap so I would like to ask the registrar how time we have left so that I can organise myself to see whether I have to skip some documents or whether I can go through all of them. Unfortunately, General, we have to strive to save time. Well, we'll go quickly now? Let us move on to a new topic. That's the military police. Could you please look at document P00957. It's a document that was used on the 3rd of -- or, rather, on the 8th of July, 2009, in the cross-examination by Ms. Tomasegovic, and it's recorded at page 42716. It's a document, the structure of the military police of the HVO, dated the 26th of December, 1992. In the course of the examination by Ms. Tomasegovic you wanted to explain some of the documents and she wouldn't let you, and she was well within her rights because it was her cross-examination. So she didn't allow you to say everything you wanted to about some documents. So now I'm asking you about this document. Do you have anything that you want to bring the attention of the Trial Chamber to, and can we perhaps read this document in such a way that we can see who is in command of the military police units?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Page 3 of the Croatian text there are two things: The military police administration commands and controls all the units of the military police. And the last sentence is: "The military police platoons in the brigades shall carry out the orders of the brigade commander within their jurisdiction." This is what I knew about the role of the military police at the time within the HVO structure, and I have nothing else to add.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I would like you to look at document P -- or 5D00538. This document was used by the -- in the cross-examination on the 8th of July, 2009, and it's also recorded at page 2 -- at page 42716 of the transcript. General, is this a document which would be tantamount to an order, or is this a document that contains within it some efforts to impose some kind of order in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a meeting where problems are presented, in particular, in item 1, in paragraph 3 where cases of murder and robbery are mentioned, also the attack on the Rumboci hospital. It's an HVO hospital. Some insane people from the HVO targeted their own hospital and then based on this, various options are present on how to impose order. But the conclusions remain. This document is comprehensive. And the conclusions say that the military police administration has to organise some kind of training and that the military police administration has to specify the rights of the military police in the exercise of their duties. Well, I don't want to go into this document. It's a comprehensive document a very detailed document. All you need to do is just read it to see what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: But it's not an order?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now I would you to look at P05381. It's a document. It was used on the 7th of July, 2009, in the cross-examination. The number of the document is P05381. And the transcript page is 42640 through 42642.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Pinter, you asked a question about the time remaining. The registrar is telling me you still have one hour and seven minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well. Thank you very much. We won't have to skip any of the documents. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, the document is the one that you signed, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And can you tell us how was this document made? You didn't have an opportunity to explain that in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from Perica Turajlija who was our military policeman who stayed behind to fight unlike some of the other members of his unit who simply left the front line and then the group that remained or, rather, the whole was the ATG group, and I asked for it to be disbanded and that the members be returned to their original units because it couldn't function any more as an organised unit or group.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now would I like to 5D04394. It's a document that was also discussed on the 7th of July, 2009, and you were shown this document at page 42640. It's again another of your documents, and you weren't given an opportunity to saying something more about it apart from answering the question, so could you please tell us what was it that you wanted to say about this document?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm responding to Mr. Valentin Coric, telling him that don't want to suspend, that I do not agree, that I did not allow --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: 5D, 5D04394. 5D. It's a Defence document. Yes. General, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he was the only one who stayed at the front line. The rest fled. And what is important about this document is to say that I cannot punish individuals who belonged to another establishment chain, and in this case, it's the military police. So a unit attached to my units from the military police, I cannot sanction them. And that is why I say to Mr. Valentin Coric, "Well, do your duty." And I list here all those who refuse to obey Mr. -- the orders, Mr. Andabak and then some people who went AWOL, and Mr. Turajlija was their commander, and some people who stopped the German humanitarian aid or did something, so it is the duty of the commander at whatever level to inform the structure that this unit belongs to the other chain of command, in other words. And I'm telling him, "Well, I am telling you what was wrong, and please take appropriate action." There's nothing else I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now I would like you to look at document P04262. It's a document that was used in the cross-examination on the 9th of July this year. The transcript page is 42833, and this document was discussed in the cross- examination. You wanted to tell us something about the reasons why this order was issued, as far as you know, and please share that with us now.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the problem was when a certain structure was not functioning, and you are the last in the food chain. The buck stops at you when it comes to solving problems. And then you accept bypassing the system to avoid greater evil. That doesn't mean that the system doesn't function any more. It's warning. In this order, actually, it's not an order but a warning issued by General Petkovic for a certain reason as is stated here. In view of the lack of efficiency in the operation of the brigade military police units -- well, I'm not going to go into reasons why that was so – commanders were addressing the military police chief. So General Petkovic says, "Well, take things into your own hands. Appoint these people, because all this moaning and whining serves no purpose." I was in disagreement with General Petkovic, because it was my position that the system could be bypassed but without the command part except in a very short time period. And on the other hand, I fully understood what he did, and I didn't revoke his order, his warning, although as his superior, I was well within my rights to did that, which means that despite a certain degree of disagreement, I also bear a certain amount of responsibility for a thing like this, because I didn't issue another piece of paper saying no, I hereby revoke this for reasons of -- because it was done in a way to -- by way of improving the system for at least a short time period, and I didn't also want to put my deputy in an unenviable position, because I considered that all of his arguments were logical. But I wouldn't have done it the same way because then you change the system and the system is quite specifically defined.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I would just like to correct the record at this page, line 4, if you see two lines -- or two dashes, this is where General Praljak's words have to be recorded. It says here who the brigade military police is to address when it encountered some problems. So, General Praljak, it doesn't say here what General Petkovic actually said in this warning. So who is the brigade military police supposed to address when it had some problems?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Just a moment. It doesn't say anything about the brigade military police talking to anyone or doing to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole document is about the brigade military police. You can see that from the subject and the whole document is about the brigade military police, and so it's not controversial.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, it is controversial because it says here that the lack of efficiency on the part of the brigade military police officers -- it says here that the lack of the brigade military police is that the commander should address. Which commanders? The commanders of the brigade military police platoons or the HVO commanders? We cannot say that on the basis of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just had a remark about the transcript, and I thought it was in your interest for General Praljak's words to be recorded accurately. I didn't want to now enter into any polemics as to what the contents of the document are.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we have marked this part and we will ask for a verification request. This is the most painless method of dealing with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General Praljak just one more question before we move on to another document. When you were at the Rama front line in the summer -- well, August, September, and October, you used the military police on the front lines.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At times.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Complete units or military police battalions and both the basic and the professional so to speak or whatever they were called, the light assault?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The professional force. Those who were trained to fight. But I simply have to say this sentence is very clear. So it often occurs that the lack of efficiency on the military police units in the brigade -- in the brigades, the commanders, address the military police chief, the commanders of those units of the military police address them, and this is the accurate depiction, and General Petkovic says, "Well take it all and do it yourself."

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Why doesn't General Petkovic issue an order but a warning?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he couldn't issue an order because it would be outside of his scope of exercise of command, but he says, "Well deal with it any which way you can so that it can finally start functioning."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters remark the speakers are again speaking very fast.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now I would like you to look at document P03934. It was discussed, it was shown to you on the 7th of July, 2009, at page 42642, line 6. In this document, General, I would like you to say in item 2 when is it says "Units and crews at VP," what does it say, VP?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military police. So it's not military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Firing position.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, firing position. If you have a VP of the artillery, that's a firing position of the artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Pinter. I do not understand. The answer, I believe it is line 18, that the answer: "Military police. So it is not military police." Now, it is either military police or not a military police. What was the answer, really, is my question. In the English transcript, I said: "Military police." Full sentence. Full stop. And the second sentence: "So it's in the military police." I really don't understand this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the document, P03934, document -- VP, in brackets, means "firing position," "vatreni polozaj," and has nothing to do with military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, open document P00460, please. You were questioned on the document by Judge Antonetti, on the 17th of June this year. The transcript page is 41000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, General, I'm coming back one step. I'm a bit amazed about this answer to the point raised by Judge Prandler. If VP here suddenly, surprisingly, exceptionally does not mean military police but firing position, I fail to understand how one gives orders to fire firing position. Firing positions are locations and not commanders of something. So this needs some more explanation if VP here suddenly is to have quite a different meaning from what it usually has.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not a new meaning. It's that I indicated item 2 of this document to the general. I point that out. And in point 2 it says: "Units and crews on the VP ..." and in item 1 it says: "The shift on the use of the front line and firing positions."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I apologise. If I had studied the document more carefully, my question would not have come up. It was superfluous. I apologise. It's a bit due to the general speed we are running in, but that's my fault.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we have to move at speed, at high speed, if we want to finish the job by the time that we have allotted.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Anyway, P00460 is the next document I'd like to look at. It's a document that was shown to you by Judge Antonetti. However, His Honour used P00459. They are two identical documents, in actual fact, but P0040 is already an exhibit; whereas document P00459 is not an exhibit, and the Judge was surprised how come that document wasn't used. Now, what I'd like to ask you now in that regard and based on that document, General, is this: You didn't complete your explanation of this convoy titled Merhamet. So could you tell us what you wanted to explain with that -- respect to that portion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a one sentence. In the hundreds of documents that we've seen in the 92 binders that we brought in the courtroom about the overall assistance given by the Republic of Croatia to Bosnia and Herzegovina, rather, the BH Army and the Muslim people, when we had the document we constantly, during this period of time, in one way or another, first of all legally and then we smuggled weapons to the BH Army, passing the HVO units; because in a war it would be completely impossible to explain to somebody fighting alongside you in the HVO that his son would be killed or wounded by weapons which the Republic of Croatia and Franjo Tudjman, Gojko Susak, Slobodan Praljak, Jadranko Prlic, Bruno Stojic, Milivoje Petkovic, and Valentin Coric of the people here would let weapons through before the conflict, during the conflict, and after the conflict. And this was smuggled in through Merhamet, and I was aware of all this from start to finish. And it's something that one can't explain, except to say that to provide weapons to the opposite side to defend itself and then also to accuse that side to go and accuse that side of having committed a crime with intent to defeat that army and cut off part of the territory goes beyond the frameworks of the little reason that I have left.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. During the cross-examination recorded on pages 42265 of the transcript, if I've read the numbers out correctly, yes, I have, and later on, on several occasions and today, too, during the examination, you were asked whether any measures were taken and whether any sanctions were taken and whether an inquiry was launched into whether anybody had actually committed crimes of any kind. Now, do you have any knowledge about that? You answered all those questions, and I'd like to ask you to take a look at this next document, which is 1D02577. It's a document which is already an exhibit. It dates to September 1994. You've already seen the document, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So you're well-acquainted with it. Now, do you know, do you have any knowledge about the verification of all the events that -- all the events were investigated that were reported and uncovered and that proceedings were taken in this regard?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can tell you is the following, and I'm testifying about this once again under oath, under the solemn declaration, as Judge Antonetti would say, and here's my testimony I -- I don't know that I or any of the other accused anywhere, at any time, or any service within the HVO, would try to hide an event without describing it, without reporting it. Now, what seems to be the most difficult thing in this trial is that it's difficult to understand how you can put your wishes into practice and do what you want to do. And when we became more powerful and had more resources and when these crimes were reported, then you could resort to legal resources and deal with the matter. So I'm saying that to the best of my knowledge, none of the five - as to Pusic, he wasn't anybody who I'd ever met before - none of us ever hid anything and you could see that from the documents. Everything was described precisely as it happened. And Judge Antonetti asked, for example: If somebody wanted to do something, could they hide it? Well, yes, but nothing was hidden. And when the time came to deal with the chaos and increase the power that you had because you can't give somebody responsibility if you don't provide him with the power necessary. You can't tell him to dig a hundred hectares without providing him with the right tools. So there was no cover-up. Everything was verified and investigated and people were taken to court as is the case today too. They were prosecuted. And the difference between observing that something had been done and to establish who the perpetrator was requires time and resources. You have to prove it and so on and so forth, and that's all I have to say on that subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's move on to the next document which is P03803. Now, Judge Trechsel asked you, on the 31st of August this year, whether Ivica Lucic, who is mentioned in the document linked to the meeting in Gornji Vakuf on the 16th of January, 1993, whether it was Ivica Lucic who was the head of SIS; and your answer was, to the best of your knowledge, there were two or more individuals with the same name, Ivica Lucic. Now, take a look at this document, please, which is dated the 30th of July, 1993, and you will see that it is about the appointment of the Eugen Kvaternik Bugojno Brigade and the relieving the duty of the brigade commander, and it also deals with Ivica Lucic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes that's right. I subsequently remembered that I do know this particular Ivica Lucic, the brigade commander. I didn't remember it at the time, but I do know the man. And it's not the Ivica Lucic who was the head of SIS.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes that's within the structure of the armed forces. Ivica Lucic from the armed forces; right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the HVO Army, not the armed forces, the army. The armed forces includes everyone, whereas this is the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: On the 7th of September, you were asked by Judge Antonetti whether during the time that you were commander of the HVO there were any conflicts with the VRS. Look at document 3D03747 now, please, in order to answer that, and tell us about the signatories of this document and the positions that the document refers to. Does it refer to the Army of Republika Srpska or does it refer to the BH Army or both perhaps?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is operations report dated the 9th of August, signed by Ivan Primorac and Mr. -- Colonel Zvonko Skender. It's the same Mr. Skender, who -- well, he is a colonel here, an HVO colonel, but he was also a colonel of the legion of honour. He was a member for 33 years, and he arrived after he retired. And this document in item 7 speaks about the fact that there were shortcomings at the separation line and the front line, the military line or whatever you'd like to call it. And it goes on to say what the positions were facing the Chetniks as they call them and then it goes on to say which features and elevations and so on. So it's the line from Stolac or around Stolac which is being held facing the Chetniks, both the men and materiel and everything else that you need for defence purposes. And it says here that the Chetniks' forces were at Kobiljaca, Kamena, Donje Brdo and so on, and then it goes on to speak of the Muslim forces and explains in the same way where their -- where the lines were facing the Muslims because unfortunately in that area and at that time the HVO was fighting two adversaries, both of them attacking it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A point in the transcript. We read on page 69, line 23, that Mr. Skender was a member of the Legion [Realtime transcript read in error "region"] of Honour and probably it was legion that one should read here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I hear that Mr. Praljak confirms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it 5.30? I think it's time for a coffee break. 20 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We resume. Mrs. Pinter, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, we both have to curb our proclivity to rush because the French booth has experienced great problems because of our speed. We will have to make pauses, we will have to speak slower because we want everything to go on the record. We talked about 3D03747, and I would like to ask you to give us your answer. It is unclear what you say at page 70. You say "military lines" or whatever it is that you call them, and then you go on to say what the positions were facing the Chetniks, as they called them "Chetniks." Who is "they?" Because its not on the report that it's "they."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the Republika Srpska Army, and in this document the signatories refer to it as the Chetnik forces, which are deployed in the Stolac area and to the south in Kobiljaca. Comovi -- I think it's actually Comovi, Kamena, Donje Brdo. Well, these are obviously hills, elevations. So this document proves my point, and that is that at that time the HVO had its combat positions facing the Republika Srpska Army and that the war was being waged there at Livno, Tomislavgrad, Rama, and further up from Gornji Vakuf towards Kupres and then on the other side from Stolac to the south. And also to the north, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. Now I would like you to look at document 3D02322. At transcript page 43678, you were asked about document P04142, and that's the plan and programme for the basic military training and education of soldiers. And why in this plan and programme, why didn't it include training about international humanitarian law and laws of war. And document 3D0322 contains also your memo or, rather, your signature is on it. It's dated the 26th of September, 1993. So could you please tell us what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's document 02763.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes. You're entirely right. This one doesn't have -- or, rather, it has a Croatian translation, but to save some time let us move on to 3D02763, and then you can use it to explain the previous document.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I received a letter from the Red Cross in order to be able to organise yet another in a whole series of seminars on international humanitarian law for HVO officers. Of course, I responded in the affirmative that we accepted the offer, but I want to note, Ms. Pinter, that in the training plan it is not explicitly listed, but humanitarian law was dealt with, and in several places you have a discussion of a humane warfare, how to fight humanely and the meaning of human life, and I think that this seminar was held on the 14th of October, if I remember correctly, as soon as the circumstances in the theatre of war allowed it. It's 3D0838.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: No, it's not 3D, it's 4D00838.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in document 4D00838, we have an order by General Petkovic stating that in Tomislavgrad, in Citluk Hotel, there would be a seminar and all available officers, about 40 to 50 officers and NCOs only from that operational zone were sent there to hear all that again, although I state that from the beginning of the war this was done through those booklets and seminars and through "Hrvatski Vojnik" journal, that every soldier was aware, was taught the basic tenets that everybody has to comply with in a war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us move on to the next document, and I will list the following documents that were used on the 8th of September 2009 in re-cross by the Stojic Defence, and you were shown 3D1104, P05104, and P05188, and they pertained to an order, your order, forwarding Mate Boban's order related to the -- I have to repeat the first number. It's 3D01104. In your answers, when Mr. Stringer and Ms. Nozica asked you some questions, you explained this order. So I don't want to go into documents with you. I just referred to them so that we can all refresh our memory, but I want to ask you whether the Main Staff appointed, recommended, and removed from office persons who were in charge -- who were charged with securing military investigative prisons and detention centres.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did the Main Staff appoint or discharge from office the wardens of the detention centres?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did the Main Staff ever receive any reports about the conditions in the prisons and detention centres?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Did the Red Cross, the international organisations, ever directly follow up with the Main Staff or submit reports about the conditions in the prisons and detention centres? Did they send them to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have been warned that I have to repeat the 3D number. It's 3D1104. And the other two numbers. So P05014 and P05188. Well, General, I think we discussed the documents, and there's no need for us to elaborate any further unless you want to add something, so I would like to now move on to document P06937. This document was discussed at page 41535, 41842 through 41843 on the 23rd of June, 2009, and also in the course of the cross-examination by Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: The counsel is really kindly asked to speak slower when listing numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So as regards to document P06937, please just bear in mind the log-book number, the reference number which is in the upper left-hand corner of this document. utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an order by Zlatan Mijo Jelic. Responsible person is Zoran Stegar, and Branko Sliskovic was in receipt of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: The reference number, the log-book number?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]

utterances.text: In document P07878, it's a document from 1994, right at the beginning of that year. It is not stated anywhere that you gave your approval or anything of the sort, that you authorised the release of Ismet Kero; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, anyone anywhere in any way, it's a forgery, and I've already said everything I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, you did say everything you had, but we had to go through this document to see that we have one and the same number for two different documents, and it actually belonged to this other document and not to the one that is purportedly signed by you.
