utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most of my documents were orders, but if I didn't issue those documents, I participated in something or I agreed with it or approved with it -- approved it. Well, you can't see it here. Somebody simply forged my signature, General Slobodan Praljak, and you don't know what this actually is, what's indicated by the signature. Ms. Pinter, I really don't have anything else to say about it. I wasn't there. I didn't write it and ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I'm just waiting for the transcript, not because I think that you have to say anything else. I just want everything to be on the report. Now I would like you to look at document P06524. Mr. Stringer asked you some questions about this document at page 44463, line 22, and the Prosecutor put it to you that this order was drafted and that it contains an order for the destruction of the Old Bridge. And now I would like you to look at it and to tell us something about this document, because you didn't have an opportunity to state your view, whether this is an order to destroy the Old Bridge. You would really have to have that document in front of you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, one has nothing to do with the other. Here it is only stated that plans should be made for some attacks, for some offensive actions, in order to tie down the BH Army units lest they should move to another area which they would be able to take piecemeal from the hands of the HVO defending those areas as it happened in Kakanj, and then there was peace. And Konjic, and then there was peace. And then Vitez before that and then there was peace. They would always take a piece of territory and then there would be peace. And it says -- it tells us that the theatre of war is a whole, and never in the history of warfare planning an offensive action had nothing to do with the destruction of bridges. Even if you assume that an action was to be launched to take East Mostar or to liberate it, whatever way you want it, you can't destroy the bridge which you would use to cross over. In the history of warfare, bridges are always destroyed after a retreat, in any war, on the Rhine, the Remagen, and so on. There is simply no military logic to it, but these are just minor actions and planning of minor actions, and I really don't have anything else to add. This has nothing to do with the destruction of the Old Bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now that we've come to the topic of the Old Bridge, I don't have to say that it was discussed in the cross-examination. In the course of the cross-examination when the Prosecutor played the videotape P01040, you wanted the video to be rewound so that you could show some parts of the tape that you thought were important. So let's first play video P01040, which was the first video to be played.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can say here that this is obviously footage that was taken on the 18th of November. It's the fact -- could you please stop there. So that the tank -- there's no collapse of the Old Bridge. Oh, yeah. No, no, I'm sorry. Yes, so that's the 8th of November. What it's -- well, what should be noted here is that the tank shells -- and you can see that -- well, we couldn't analyse it, because we didn't have the important part of the recording, of this recording that was recorded, and that's the black smoke that His Honour Judge Antonetti noted. The tank shell does not produce any black smoke. It hits and it destroys it, and there's a dust cloud. Unfortunately since this part of the tape wasn't there, we couldn't analyse the smoke, and based on everything that I know and what you can see on the image it cannot be caused by a tank shell. It's explosive -- explosive which according to the findings of the expert and all the information was placed inside the Old Bridge. It would be good had we had it at the time, because then greater experts than I am would have been able to tell us based on the smoke what kind of explosive it was, but I think that even laypersons can see that this was not a tank shell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well. We can play the tape on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you can see quite clearly where the explosion was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Is that the pause, when you said there was a lull?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that -- what I assume, and I think it's fair that this wouldn't have been broadcast by any major television channel, so this was spliced. He -- the person who showed this probably linked the two together; the explosion that didn't topple the bridge and the one that did on a tape filmed by somebody else. So all this is montage. It has all been edited. You can see that if you look at the smoke and now he has superimposed one over the other to get it in a shorter space, and we notice that a portion was missing. We didn't have the breath of it all. It was this Mr. Schotte or Scott or Scotts or whatever.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop there. Now, Your Honours, this is not a tank shell. This certainly isn't a tank shell, which means that somebody else, without a doubt, was targeting the Old Bridge. And as this is a much smaller calibre, because obviously not much damage was done, it couldn't have been a shot from the position where the tank was at.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, General, for the record I'd like to say that we're looking at IC00574, chapter 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. Move on. Now, this shell, judging by anything that the human eye can see and that you can conclude, is coming somewhere from the north, from a northerly direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want this to be on the transcript. We see, and we will show it again because we have enough time, we clearly see that there is an impact with a flash, but the impact and the flash are on the other side of the bridge. We need to see this again, and please look carefully.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we go back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm claiming, Your Honours and Ms. Pinter, is that there is no position from the north from which the HVO could target the Old Bridge. Who was doing the firing, I don't know, but you can go to Mostar, I can bring in the large map that I showed, the 2 by 2 metres map if Their Honours want to see it. There is no HVO position on the northern side of the bridge for this kind of projectile to be firing. Now, who did the firing, I don't know, so one must distinguish between the two, who was doing what from where?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we play it again maybe ten times so that everyone sees -- sees correctly and that there's no doubt left?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, perhaps for the record you could describe what we just saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. I would like to note something on the transcript. We see two tires hanging on the other side of the bridge, and there -- and because of the fire they're going to oscillate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right now. Actually, one is actually going to fall into the water. There were two tires hanging. The shot comes from the north, and one of the tire falls into the water and the others are just -- the other is just hanging on, and they're not facing us. They're behind us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing to add there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Perhaps for the record just it is correct to add that these shots purportedly coming from the other side, perhaps from the north, do not create any visible damage to the bridge. They seem to be a relatively light calibre. What one sees is light, and it affects the tires, but one does not see any stones falling down or anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can we move on? Should we show more of the tape?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, no. We've actually seen something there coming from the south. This isn't a tank either. So there was somebody else shooting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a tank, and quite obviously there, well, it's a large plot surrounding this bridge. They're shooting from the south and from the north. See for yourselves. May we see the section where the bridge actually falls into the water?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the destruction of the Old Bridge on the 9th, taken by that Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I ask perhaps a few questions about the tank? Do you have an idea of what type of tank it is that was shooting? You must, because otherwise you could not be too precise about the ammunition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ninety-nine per cent certainty it was a T-55 tank of Russian manufacture, a T-55, most probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that tank equipped with a machine-gun coaxial to the main barrel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Is it -- is it possible that what we see as lights that are rejected, which is an ammunition that doesn't do damage to the bridge itself, that it is what is sometimes used, a tracing bullet. In order to be economic with the heavy stuff one first shoots a lighting, small calibre, to see whether the aim is right, and then after -- afterwards one shoots the big barrel. Is that a possible explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour Judge Trechsel. The tank does have a 7.62 calibre, I think, on it, a machine-gun which is too small a calibre to send anything towards the bridge. So this is a higher calibre than the 7.62 that we saw, the red. So with a machine-gun on a tank, which is defence towards an infantry, at this distance where the tank is there's absolutely no military connection there, nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Are we on IC00574, chapter 3? We are.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: There's no need to go into that now. Very well. Now we go to IC00820.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I still have a question about the tank. I have opened the -- on the internet I have looked at the T-55. I have here T-55A, which has actually three types of ammunition for the cannon. The -- the one that one uses on armoured targets, it is sort of partly empty, and then the force is all concentrated. I'm sure you know what I mean. Then there is the normal one, and there is one that causes shrapnels to go. Would any of these ammunitions give a black smoke?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. I'm not that expert in this field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps -- perhaps it would be helpful to -- just to indicate that there were a lot of questions and something also in expert report of Dr. Jankovic on the tank shell, which was allegedly targeting the bridge. So probably the answer is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, we're now going to look at some ORF footage. IC00820. It was used together with Dr. Jankovic's testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see that again, please? Can we have the footage again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's not the beginning. I apologise, but this isn't from the beginning. Can we take it from the beginning, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That's what we have IC00820 the IC number.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is obviously what I said, the first explosion and the waterfall shown in -- or water fountain was spliced and attached to the part that was thrown out that Judge Antonetti mentioned. So can we have the continuous damage.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] IC00820 is next, please - we seem to have some technical problems - or IC00821. This was used together with Professor Jankovic as well, and it's from Television Mostar. If they manage to play that for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: General, I'm afraid we don't seem to be able to have that last tape which we planned to show. There seem to be technical difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours and everybody else in the courtroom, I'm sure you understand the problems we're having with the technical aspect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, never mind, but the camera shows -- the footage shows in continuum the water fountain, the point at the bridge where the explosion begins and after which the bridge falls down. According to all logic, there was a second explosion on the bridge, because the first did not give the desired result, and since the person didn't film the second explosion properly, he put the two together; whereas on this second IC number, we have the continuous footage of the bridge, and I have nothing further to state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. I was just suggesting that we go on, because as we will, in all probability, have an expert. We will, again, have another round of bridge destruction. Please, Ms. Pinter.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, but that was the last subject we wanted to deal with. I can see that our -- my colleagues have a happy smile on their faces. I know there are other topics that we could deal with, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the book, from the book.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. We've also prepared the book. So while we're waiting for the technicians to prepare the material, we can look at 3D00374 in our binders. It is the book by Slobodan Praljak, "How the Old Bridge Was Destroyed." And I'd like to look at 3D16-0035 of the Croatian text, and in English it is on page 3D16-0113. And on that particular page, the letters are underlined which refer to the Croatian text, the only portion in that excerpt that's been underline. Anyway, General, these are excerpts from the paper, "Oslobodjenje" of the 19th of June, 1997, and, in fact, it confirms what you've told us. Now, tell us, please, of course you saw the article later on, but did you see it as soon as it was published, as it -- when it came out?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a little later, probably, because at that time I was already troubled by the act I was held accountable for. And the protection of the Old Bridge was a concern of ours throughout the time I was there. And what's important here is the following, I'm going to read it out slowly, and I thank the interpreters: "At the moment when it happened, a camera was turned towards the bridge by a Scotsman who was in this city as member of the British Army. He was ordered by Budakovic to go to Sarajevo, accompanied by members of military security of the 4th Corps command, but instead of giving the precious document as it had been agreed to the then-director of Radio Television Bosnia and Herzegovina, he jumped on the first UNPROFOR plane and left Bosnia." Therefore -- well, Budakovic here, I think, already at that time was either the deputy commander of the 4th Corps or perhaps perform -- was acting as the 4th Corps commander. And secondly, regular British troops in that area -- there were no regular British troops in that region, because as you know, the region was under the military control -- well, I can't really say control, but supervision, or whatever, operating there on behalf of UNPROFOR was SpaBat, the Spanish Battalion. Now, Mrs. Pinter, I don't know who, I know how, Your Honours, someone wanted to prolong the war and to increase the conflict between the Croats and Muslims, and that is why they committed this act at a point in time when General Petkovic was in Split, when I was in Tomislavgrad, and when duty was being handed over. The commander of the HVO, of the Main Staff, Slobodan Praljak, did not destroy the Old Bridge in the BH Army attacks when there was absolutely justification for destroying the Old Bridge as a military target. We did not do that. We didn't destroy the hanging bridges that people used to cross over. That was not our objective or goal. That was not the kind of war we were waging. We were defending ourselves, but 20 obvious military targets in the centre of town, we did not fire at them with cannons precisely so as to avoid civilian casualties in Mostar. I am not saying that there were not any civilian casualties, but in relation to the number of soldiers killed, according to the 4th Corps commander Drekovic - he writes about this in his book - the number of civilian casualties was very small precisely because of the manner in which we engaged in warfare -- or, rather, how I led the army, commanded the army, and that would be all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Well, the transcript stopped. I don't know if everything has been interpreted. General, thank you very much for the five months that you spent in the witness stand. I would like to thank the Trial Chamber, all my colleagues. The Defence counsel has no more questions for General Praljak.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would also like to thank you for all the questions you asked me. I would like to apologise for wandering, and I would like to apologise to the interpreters. I really didn't mean it. It was just my body that refused to obey my orders of my mind. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Praljak, on Monday next week, we'll be hearing your expert witness. He will be sitting in your chair, and unfortunately you'll be back at the back of the room. I believe that Mr. Scott has something to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something to say. If at any point in this trial you want to ask any additional questions, I am at your disposal. I'm ready to go back to the witness stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I took due note of this. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, and in terms of Mr. Praljak's last comment, why are we not surprised. I'm afraid I need to try -- perhaps try the Chamber's patience a bit late on this Thursday afternoon and perhaps other counsel's as well because I'm sure everyone is anxious to leave the courtroom. However, I do have to make a submission with the greatest respect in connection with the ruling the Chamber made earlier today. And if nothing else, I just want the record to be clear about the Prosecution's position on the matter. And this is in connection with the time for cross-examination of the Praljak witnesses that are scheduled over the next few weeks. Mr. President, Your Honours, and I'm going to look at my notes in rather detail in order not to use any excess words as possible in the time that we have, so forgive me if I follow my notes rather closely, perhaps, than usual. Mr. President, Your Honours, there's never been a previous ruling, and it has never been the practice in this case that the time estimate for cross-examination was required to be placed in the notice requesting cross-examination. That has never been the prior ruling or practice of this Chamber. I went through all the submissions requesting -- all the filings requesting cross-examination since the trial began, this afternoon, by the Defence and by the Prosecution. That's never been done. The Chamber will not find a single filing in which the request for time has been put in one of those notices. This is the first time that's ever happened. Secondly, with an expert witness and a Rule 92 ter witness, there has never been -- it has never been required by the Defence or the Prosecution to date, it has never been required that the opposing party, be it the Defence or the Prosecution, had to make a special showing to justify more time for cross-examination than direct examination. It has been universally recognised that given the fundamental fact that the tendering party is putting in most -- much if not most of the direct examination on paper, be that a report, an expert report, or a statement, it's only a matter of fundamental fairness that the opposing party be given more time for cross-examination than direct. That has been the consistent practice in this Chamber since April 2006 until today. This has been the practice to date. It certainly was the practice throughout the Prosecution case, which worked to the benefit of the Defence, and we provided to the Chamber information demonstrating this in our filing yesterday. It is absolutely clear, the record speaks for itself, that in all instances of 92 ter witnesses and experts that they've been -- the opposing party has been provided more time if needed or requested to conduct the cross-examination. This is a new and different situation. I'm sorry to say, Your Honour, but I have to make a record, this is another situation where the rules applying to the Prosecution are different than rules that apply to the Defence during the Prosecution case. The Prosecution case is being treated to a disadvantage, and the rules have changed. The reality is there is no prejudice to the Defence in this situation. We have two witnesses, each of whom are scheduled for an entire court week. The time is there. The request has been made consistent with past practice, and with due respect, Your Honour, the Prosecution feels it has been treated -- it is being treated very unfairly in this situation. So in that respect, Your Honour, and I guess it's become, perhaps, a bit of a dirty word, but if the Chamber wants to call it a request for consideration, then there it is. But the rules -- the Prosecution submits that the rules have changed to the Prosecution's disadvantage. We do need adequate time to conduct a meaningful cross-examination of these two witnesses, and we ask to be granted more time to do so. Obviously any counsel, again, be that the Defence or the Prosecution, has to prepare an examination in advance, and that's why I'm on my feet at this late hour and not raising this on Monday afternoon for the first time. Therefore, Your Honour, that's our submission. I appreciate the Chamber giving me the opportunity to raise it at this hour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will not respond to this. I will just say one sentence. The Trial Chamber did, well I can't now claim with certainty but I think it was April this year, ruled to accept the experts' testimony that was proposed and also allotting the time to the parties. Until yesterday or the day before yesterday, which was when the first proposal was made, the Prosecution just sat there not reacting. It could have sought to review or reconsider -- the reconsideration of the decision within a reasonable time, but they failed to do so. They could have appealed against the decision, yet they failed to do that either. And now, once we've made our plans for the stay of the witness here and all the other witnesses based on the known parameters that we received through the decisions, through this particular decision, and we knew that nobody wanted anything outside of the decision, nobody applied for additional time and nobody, in fact, questioned the decision at all, we had to and we could do a detailed plan. I don't see that there's any reason for the Trial Chamber to amend or change its decision in any anyway. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: With the leave of my learned friend before he rises to respond to the submissions of Mr. Kovacic, it is my submission that all of this is unnecessary, to say the least. In the oral ruling of this morning, a unanimous Bench dismissed the Prosecution's application on the grounds that it was, amongst other things, a motion for reconsideration. Now, as far as the record, making a record is concerned, I don't know if it's a Grammy record or a CD, but as far as a court record is concerned, my learned friend, Mr. Stringer, did stand up after the Presiding Judge gave his ruling to make further submissions; and once again those further submissions, those further objections, were dismissed by the Bench. Here we are at the end of the day for the third time, it seems to me, revisiting an issue that has been judiciously determined not once but on three previous occasions if one counts the decision this morning as a reconsideration. Now, Your Honours, the rules do allow for an application for leave to appeal. That can be done in writing. But to keep having this tennis match, this ping-pong against judicial rulings is rather indulgent. And I do know that all sides, not just my learned friend, Mr. Scott, all sides in this courtroom have been guilty of indulgence and self-indulgence on various occasions to varying degrees. But this kind of ping-pong match is hardly conducive, in my respectful submission, to the proper determination of this matter in an expeditious manner. And for those reasons, I would ask that the submission is not only inappropriate but should be summarily dismissed. If the Prosecution have further objections, of course, an application for leave to appeal can be put in writing. Your Honour, those are my submission on this matter. I am grateful.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please allow the Petkovic Defence to also state its views. I would like to answer, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me for a moment ... [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am entitled -- Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you said something. The Defence has responded and they're not finished because Mrs. Alaburic would also like to say something, and then you will take the floor again and give her a chance to tell her position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [Previous translation continues] ... My concern, Your Honour, is that this is what always happens. As I make a point, the Prosecution makes a point, and then we run through a series of Defence -- everyone one the Defence side, with great respect, pops up and then my time is gone as it will be tonight. And this is what's happened a number of times in the history of this case, so I'm making that point but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will have the time. You will have the time. I can stay until midnight to listen to you, if necessary. Mrs. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Petkovic Defence would like to express its understanding for the arguments proffered by the colleagues from the Prosecution when they asked for more time to examine General Praljak's expert witnesses. The understanding is there because we presented virtually identical arguments when expert witnesses called by the Prosecution were heard. Other Defence teams presented similar arguments. Let me remind you about the arguments by the Prlic Defence for the -- for expert witness Tomanovic, and so on and so forth. My learned friends for the Prosecution have never expressed their understanding or agreement with our objections, but they object pose them strenuously. I would like to remind the Trial Chamber about some developments in this courtroom which completely refute what Mr. Scott has told us a little while ago, that it has been a practice of this Tribunal and that now this practice is being changed in the course of the Defence case. Let me give you just one example. It is the Prosecution military expert, Mr. Pringle. The Trial Chamber had ruled that four hours would be allotted for the examination-in-chief and that all the Defence teams would have a total of four hours for the cross-examination. General Petkovic's Defence applied to be given additional time, elaborating topic by topic in greater detail its arguments and also providing documents that we wanted to ask expert Pringle about; so we asked for additional time, and we elaborated the reasons and documented the reasons with a set of documents. Our request was denied so that the Petkovic Defence, in the end, received one hour, out of a total of four hours allotted to all the Defence teams, for the examination of witness Pringle. The Petkovic Defence then asked -- sought leave to appeal against the decision of the Trial Chamber. The Prosecution did not support us in our request, although the motion was based on the arguments that are very similar to the ones presented by our colleagues from the opposite side today. Our motion was denied, and we were not granted leave to appeal against the decision. I would also like to remind the Trial Chamber that the Petkovic Defence also sought additional time for the examination of expert witness Bruno Stojic, elaborating the topics and documents it wanted to show to the witness and discuss with him, and it was also important to did that on time. I would like to remind you that we did that two months before the witness was supposed to appear in the courtroom. So everything that Mr. Scott said about the practice of the Tribunal so far to the detriment of the Prosecution, which is now being changed, purportedly again, to the detriment of the Prosecution this is just a misrepresentation of facts. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm going to start with the last, and I have great respect for my friend Ms. Alaburic, but I couldn't disagree more with some of the things she just said. There was no misrepresentation involved. I will come back to that in a moment. Let me respond very briefly to the points made. In fairness, Your Honour, let me be as transparent as possible, given what had been established practice. I believe and I will take responsibility, I believed that as the time of the actual appearances of these witnesses came closer in time, it provided some additional -- request was made ahead of time was consistent with what I believed to be established practice, and what I still submit has been established practice up until now, that there would be at least a serious consideration given based on a fundamental principle that the cross-examining party concerning an expert or a 92 ter witness is given more time to conduct cross-examination. I thought that would be the rule. If the rules have changed, then, in the future, I'll try to see that our team and myself conducts itself differently, but that was based -- expectations do develop in a case over a three-year period. There are establish practice. There are expectation that is come into play and I believe that it's only fair for the parties to be able to have some predictability as to what the rules of the game are, and in this case it has not been. Secondly -- next, in response to Mr. Kovacic, this -- this request has absolutely no impact whatsoever on scheduling, none, zero. So with all due respect to Mr. Kovacic, it's completely disingenuous to stand up and say this, quote, late request will impact the scheduling in the case. Each witness -- each of these witnesses is scheduled for an entire court week, four days, with no other witness scheduled around them. So whether or not -- whatever the Chamber does, but I want the point to be clear, whatever the Chamber does, it will have no impact on scheduling, no other witness is coming to The Hague, no other witness will be delayed, no other witness will be asked to stay over. It is completely incorrect for counsel to suggest that this will impact scheduling one iota. Next, in terms of Mr. Khan's comments about Mr. Stringer, I certainly heard Mr. Stringer's comments, and while he addressed another matter, there were no additional submissions on this point. I take full responsibility for making the submissions on this point. In light of the Chamber's ruling, Mr. Stringer quite correctly did say that as to the future Petkovic witness, that there would be an additional filing made in these circumstances. That's what he addressed. I'm the only one addressing this particular point, and, again, I take responsibility for that. Again, I disagree with Ms. Alaburic's submissions. I think there has been time, in fact, various times, in fact, in the last three-plus years that the Prosecution has been understanding of Defence positions and has, in fact, supported Defence positions on various occasions. Thank you, Your Honour, for allowing our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The time has come to close the session. Would I like to thank the interpreters for their work. I thank all of you, and I -- we will reconvene on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 14th day of September, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25
